candidates.attacker_control: Any SSH client that completes authentication with the server controls all forwarding requests: it chooses the global `tcpip-forward` requests (client `-R`) and `direct-tcpip` channel-open requests (client `-L`), including bind addresses, ports and connection targets.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Verified `TcpForwardingFilter.canListen` is documented as 'the session may listen for inbound connections' and `canConnect` as 'the session may create an outbound connection' (TcpForwardingFilter.java lines 52-68 and 136-153); verified the only caller tying `tcpip-forward` to the filter is `DefaultForwarder.localPortForwardingRequested` -> `canListen` and the only caller tying `direct-tcpip` to the filter is `TcpipServerChannel.doInit` -> `canConnect(Direct, ...)`, with no local/remote swap elsewhere; verified `AllowTcpForwardingValue` is the sole `TcpForwardingFilter` implementation and is only reached from server config parsing; verified `ALL`/`NONE` are correct and that `docs/technical/tcpip-forwarding.md` defines local forwarding as client `-L` and remote forwarding as client `-R`. Counter-hypothesis that MINA intentionally defines these values from the client's perspective was considered: that would make the values correct for a client-side filter but they are placed in and used by server-side `sshd_config` parsing (`org.apache.sshd.server.config`), contradicting the cited OpenSSH semantics.
candidates.impact: Authorization-policy bypass: with the restrictive `AllowTcpForwarding local` setting, any authenticated user can still compel the SSH server to bind TCP listening sockets (potentially on wildcard/all interfaces, subject to OS permissions) and tunnel inbound connections back to the client, enabling firewall/NAT traversal and exposure of services in the server network. With `AllowTcpForwarding remote`, the server will instead open outbound connections to arbitrary hosts chosen by the client, providing a pivot into networks reachable only from the server. In both cases the capability the operator believed disabled remains enabled, while the capability the operator expected to allow is broken.
candidates.prerequisites: The server is configured with the granular policy `AllowTcpForwarding local` or `AllowTcpForwarding remote` (e.g. `-o AllowTcpForwarding=local` or via `SshServerConfigFileReader.resolveTcpForwardingFilter`) and the client is authenticated. `yes`/`all` and `no`/`none` are unaffected.
candidates.root_cause: In `AllowTcpForwardingValue`, `LOCAL` returns `canListen = true` (server accepts client `tcpip-forward` requests and binds listening sockets) and `canConnect = false` (server rejects client `direct-tcpip` channel opens, i.e. client local forwarding), while `REMOTE` returns the exact mirror image (`canListen = false`, `canConnect = true`). Per `sshd_config(5)` (the man page the file itself cites) and per the `TcpForwardingFilter` javadoc in the same snapshot, `local` must allow only `direct-tcpip` (server connects out) and `remote` must allow only `tcpip-forward`/listeners. The granular values are therefore inverted; only `yes`/`all` and `no`/`none` behave as documented.
candidates.title: AllowTcpForwarding 'local'/'remote' policies are mapped to the opposite forwarding directions
candidates.trace: 1) `AllowTcpForwarding=<value>` is parsed by `SshServerConfigFileReader.resolveTcpForwardingFilter` (lines 129-134) into `AllowTcpForwardingValue`. 2) For a client `-R` (remote forwarding) the server's `TcpipForwardHandler.process` (lines 61-73) builds an `SshdSocketAddress` and calls `forwarder.localPortForwardingRequested(...)`, which in `DefaultForwarder` (lines 658-670) consults `filter.canListen(...)` and, if true, binds a listening socket (`doBind`, line 682). With `AllowTcpForwarding local` the inverted mapping returns `canListen=true`, so the server binds and accepts inbound connections that the administrator intended to forbid. 3) For a client `-L` (local forwarding) the server receives a `direct-tcpip` channel open; `TcpipServerChannel.doInit` (lines 155-190) consults `filter.canConnect(Type.Direct, ...)` and denies the channel when false. With `AllowTcpForwarding local` the inverted mapping returns `canConnect=false`, so the operation the administrator intended to permit is refused. `AllowTcpForwarding remote` produces the mirror-image behavior (outbound connections permitted, listeners denied).
candidates.unverified: No runtime/configuration test was executed, so the end-to-end behavior was not observed; the upstream history could not be inspected to determine whether this mapping is the original upstream code or a local regression, and if MINA deliberately defines `local`/`remote` from the client's perspective the practical impact would be a functional mismatch rather than a policy bypass. Only the enumeration constant bodies were traced; deployment code that swaps the values before installing the filter was not found but cannot be fully excluded.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-863 Incorrect Authorization (server-side forwarding policy bypass)

coverage_summary: get_source_scope reports 1110 model-visible source files, no over-size/sensitive-name/symlink exclusions and binary NUL-byte filtering only. I reviewed the whole-file inventory and read/traced security-relevant code across sshd-common (host-key provider, key/certificate parsing, Buffer/Signature/KeyUtils, RootedFileSystemProvider, IO helpers), sshd-core (session/KEX handling, user authentication, public-key/certificate paths, forwarding filters, TCP/IP forward handlers, SFTP-in-core helpers), sshd-scp (ScpCommand, ScpHelper, resolvers/opener), sshd-sftp (server subsystem helper and SftpSubsystem, file accessor), sshd-cli, sshd-git, sshd-contrib, sshd-ldap and sshd-spring-sftp. Test sources are not present in the snapshot, so behavior could not be cross-checked against unit tests.
limitations: Read-only review with no execution: no build, unit test, or runtime forwarding negotiation was performed, so the finding is not runtime-confirmed.

Not every one of the 1110 files was read line-by-line; coverage prioritized authentication, key exchange, forwarding policy, filesystem confinement, SCP/SFTP file operations and configuration parsing.

Upstream repository history, tags and later fixes were not available, so it was not possible to determine whether the inverted mapping is original upstream code or a snapshot-local regression, nor to compare against the fixed version.
Tests are excluded from the visible snapshot, removing a useful source of intended-behavior evidence for AllowTcpForwarding semantics.
Synthetic or generated code variations cannot be ruled out; only textual/structural evidence in this snapshot was used.

rejected_leads.reason: `SimpleGeneratorHostKeyProvider` already wraps `ObjectInputStream` in a `ValidatingObjectInputStream` that only resolves an allow-list of classes (`resolveClass` at lines 145-155) and writes keys in OpenSSH format, so the known deserialization vector appears mitigated in this snapshot.

No `kex-strict-c/s-v00@openssh.com` handling exists anywhere in the tree, so sessions are theoretically open to prefix truncation when using affected ciphers/MACs. This is a protocol-capability absence spread across KEX proposal/session handling rather than a localized source defect, and packet-sequence handling was not verifiable without runtime negotiation; weaker and less localizable than the chosen candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: SCP receive path lacks explicit containment checks for peer-supplied file names
rejected_leads.reason: `LocalFileScpTargetStreamResolver.resolveTargetStream` (lines 71-89) and `ScpFileOpener.resolveIncomingFilePath` (lines 72-118) join the peer-supplied `name` onto the target directory without an explicit `normalize()/startsWith(root)` guard, so names containing `..` or absolute paths are a plausible traversal vector. No corroborating TODO/known-fix marker exists and the code matches the project's long-standing behavior, so it stayed a rejected lead.

`UserAuthPublicKey.doAuth` (lines 95-116) contains a TODO stating that the certificate CA key is not validated against authorized_keys/TrustedUserCAKeys. This is explicitly documented incomplete functionality in the snapshot, and the certificate signature is verified for host certificates (`DHGClient.verifyCertificate`); exploiting it requires a trusted-key-setup assumption, so it was not selected.
Version pinning was noted in pom.xml, but dependency CVEs are outside the repository's own source logic and could not be validated from the snapshot.

summary: Repository is Apache MINA sshd at a ~2.9.2/2.10.0-development snapshot (pom version 2.9.2; CHANGES.md "Planned for next version" ends at SSHD-1307/GH-266). I reviewed the security-relevant paths around KEX/host-key handling, server authentication, forwarding filters, virtual/rooted filesystems, SCP receive paths, SFTP server path handling and key/certificate parsing. The strongest source-level finding is an authorization-policy inversion in AllowTcpForwardingValue: the `local`/`remote` values map to the opposite forwarding directions from the OpenSSH `sshd_config(5)` semantics that the class itself references, so a restrictive `AllowTcpForwarding local`/`remote` policy still leaves the opposite (explicitly denied) forwarding capability enabled. The known legacy host-key Java-deserialization issue (GH-229/CVE-2022-45047) is already mitigated in this tree, and the strict-KEX (Terrapin) mitigation is absent but that is a protocol-wide property with weak local source evidence, so neither was chosen.
